text: For strong root establishment and high yields, Robusta coffee needs fertile, well-aerated, well-drained, slightly acidic and deep soil containing humus. The handbook describes ideal soils as volcanic red earth or sandy loams with good structure and organic matter. Waterlogged soils and heavy clay or poorly drained soils should be avoided. The recommended soil pH range is 5.5–6.5; soil below pH 5.5 can limit crop performance and may require liming.

The recommended altitude range for Robusta coffee production is 900–1,500 metres above sea level. Altitude can influence cup profile: coffee grown at higher elevations tends to be more acidic and complex, while coffee grown at lower elevations tends to have a more intense flavour. The handbook describes Uganda as producing relatively high-altitude Robusta at an average of about 1,200 metres above sea level.

Robusta coffee is suited to warm conditions, with a recommended temperature range of 22–28°C. It tolerates heat better than Arabica coffee, but temperatures above 30°C can cause physiological problems such as flower abortion, poor fruit setting and development, and premature ripening. Photosynthesis is also reduced at these high temperatures. Frost damage can occur at temperatures around 0°C or below.

Robusta coffee requires about 1,200–1,800 mm of rainfall, distributed fairly evenly over approximately nine months. Both the total rainfall and its distribution matter. Newly planted seedlings should be irrigated or hand-watered at least twice a week when rainfall is irregular. Supplementary irrigation during dry periods can support continuous growth, more uniform flowering and good fruit formation.

Excessive drought can dehydrate coffee trees, cause leaf fall and increase attacks by pests including red spider mite, leaf miner, twig borer and coffee berry borer; severe stress can also lead to wilting or death. Prolonged excessive rainfall may promote vegetative growth while inhibiting or damaging flowering. Strong winds increase water loss and can break trees, increasing irrigation needs. The handbook recommends establishing windbreaks along plantation borders in especially windy locations.

Intercropping means growing coffee together with one or more other crops in the same field. While coffee is young, the spaces between rows can be used for selected food crops, including bananas, green pepper, cabbages, tomatoes, soya beans, groundnuts and non-climbing Phaseolus beans. These intercrops should be confined to the central two metres of the inter-row, leaving 0.5 metres clear between the intercrop and coffee trees. The handbook warns against continuously growing beans on the same plots, especially in humid areas, because aphid problems may occur.

Coffee–banana intercropping is a major coffee system in Uganda. Bananas can provide shade to young coffee during early establishment, but too many banana plants may compete with coffee for nutrients. The handbook recommends a banana-to-coffee ratio of 1:4: one banana plant for every four coffee bushes.

Coffee leaf rust is a leaf disease caused by the fungus Hemileia vastatrix. The UCDA handbook reports that it occurs in Robusta-growing districts in Uganda at elevations around 1,000–1,500 metres above sea level, and that some Robusta cultivars are more susceptible than others. Severe infection can cause premature leaf fall and reduced yield.

section: 7.2.2 Coffee Leaf Rust: Symptoms and spread
text: Early coffee leaf rust symptoms are pale-yellow spots on the lower surfaces of leaves. The spots enlarge and produce orange-coloured spores; older parts of lesions can become necrotic and brown. Spores may spread through wind, rain splash, insects and people. Infected seedlings or cuttings can also introduce the disease into new fields.

Coffee leaf rust causes premature defoliation and reduces the leaf area available for photosynthesis. Repeated attacks can force the plant to use stored carbohydrates to support developing berries and can contribute to the loss of fine feeder roots. As a result, coffee bushes may gradually decline, yields may fall, berries may fail to fill properly, and young berries may be shed. Infected leaves remaining on trees can provide a source of infection when rains return.

The UCDA handbook recommends good field management, beginning with proper field preparation and clean planting materials from recommended nurseries. Cultural practices such as proper pruning and weeding are part of management. Using resistant or tolerant varieties, where available, is effective. The handbook states that chemical control is not economical and is not recommended for Robusta coffee, in contrast with Arabica where rust can be very destructive.

text: The CATIE handbook identifies coffee leaf rust as a severe coffee disease reported in Sri Lanka in 1869, where the fungus was described and named Hemileia vastatrix. The manual discusses a hypothesis that the disease may have reached Sri Lanka accidentally from East Africa through movement of diseased plants, people and goods. It also notes that abundant rainfall and susceptible coffee planted in homogeneous full-sun plantations created favourable conditions for disease development.

section: Relevance and how to use the handbook
text: The CATIE manual explains that the 2012–2013 coffee leaf rust epidemic affected coffee production across Central America. It reports an average regional production reduction of about 15% for that period, with crop losses, lower income and increased unemployment. The manual emphasizes that epidemics can recur and that prevention and control measures need to be applied in a timely and effective way.

section: Chapter 2: Life cycle of the fungus
text: The CATIE handbook describes Hemileia vastatrix as a biotrophic organism: it depends on living plant tissue for nutrition. The fungus infects coffee leaves and develops through stages in the host. Understanding its life cycle and reproduction helps explain disease development and supports decisions about prevention and management.

document: Prevention and control of coffee leaf rust
text: The CATIE manual treats temperature and altitude as environmental factors influencing coffee leaf rust. Their effects should be interpreted together with local climate and farm conditions rather than as isolated variables. The handbook frames rust development as an interaction between the pathogen, the coffee plant, the environment and crop management.

document: Prevention and control of coffee leaf rust
text: The CATIE handbook cautions that the relationship between shade and coffee leaf rust is not universally negative or positive. Earlier concerns often focused on poorly designed or poorly managed shade, but research discussed in the manual found that shade can have positive relationships with rust control under some climatic conditions. Shade therefore needs to be assessed in relation to climate and how the coffee system is managed.

section: Chapter 8: Best practices for prevention and control
text: The CATIE manual organizes rust management into several complementary areas, including agronomic management, genetic control and chemical control. Agronomic management includes practices such as pruning and sucker removal, fertilization and shade management. The manual presents these as parts of an overall prevention and control approach rather than treating one practice as a complete solution.

document: Prevention and control of coffee leaf rust
text: The CATIE handbook reports that coffee varieties and hybrids with resistance or tolerance to leaf rust have been used in Central America. It cautions that resistance to one disease does not guarantee resistance to all diseases. The manual describes using different varieties in separate farm lots—selected for resistance or tolerance to different diseases—as one strategy, while noting that cup quality should also be considered.

text: The CATIE manual says coffee leaf rust is difficult to eliminate once established in an area. Severe epidemics can weaken plantations and reduce production not only during the current cycle but also in following years. The manual therefore emphasizes learning to manage the disease and applying preventive or control practices in a timely manner.
